content: Cocoa butter, also known as theobroma oil, is a pale-yellow, edible vegetable fat derived from cacao beans. It serves as the primary ingredient in the production of solid chocolate bars. To create chocolate, cocoa butter is combined with varying amounts of cocoa powder, resulting in solid chocolate pieces. This fat is extracted from cacao beans and is utilized not only in chocolate and cocoa powder production but also in pharmaceuticals, ointments, and toiletries. Cocoa butter is characterized by its mild chocolate flavor and aroma. During the processing of cacao beans, cocoa solids and cocoa butter are separated early in the procedure. These components are later recombined to manufacture standard brown chocolate bars. White chocolate, on the other hand, contains cocoa butter but does not include cocoa powder. Due to its melting temperature, cocoa butter is frequently used in pharmaceuticals as a base for suppositories. It remains stable at room temperature but melts readily at body temperature, allowing for the release of medication. Cocoa butter is one of the most stable fats available, as it contains natural antioxidants that prevent it from becoming rancid. This stability provides it with a shelf life of two to five years, making it an excellent choice for non-food applications. Its smooth texture, pleasant fragrance, and moisturizing properties make it a popular ingredient in cosmetics and skincare products, such as soaps and lotions. Cocoa butter typically has a melting point between 34 and 38 degrees Celsius (93 to 100 degrees Fahrenheit), which allows chocolate to remain solid at room temperature but melt easily in the mouth. It exhibits polymorphism, meaning it can form different crystal structures, including α, γ, β', and β crystals, with melting points of 17, 23, 26, and 35–37 degrees Celsius, respectively. The β crystal is predominantly used in chocolate production due to its higher melting point, which contributes to the desired texture, sheen, and snap of chocolate. Overheating cocoa butter can alter its crystal structure, resulting in a less stable form that melts below room temperature. However, given sufficient time, cocoa butter will naturally revert to its most stable β crystal form.
